title: The NewReno Modification to TCP's Fast Recovery Algorithm
summary: This RFC specifies the NewReno modification to TCP Fast Recovery, building on RFC 5681. It deals with partial acknowledgments, which cover new data but not all outstanding data, so several lost packets can be repaired in one recovery.

plainLanguage.summary: If several pieces of a message get lost, TCP can notice and resend them all without slowing down over and over.

questions: how does newreno handle partial acks
what is the recover variable in newreno
subtitle: How a TCP sender without SACK recovers from several lost packets in one window without timing out or shrinking its window again and again.

tldr.problem: With plain Reno fast recovery, each fast retransmit repairs only one lost packet. When several packets are lost from one window, the sender often takes a retransmit timeout, or runs several fast retransmits and window reductions.
tldr.mechanism: NewReno treats a partial acknowledgment (one that covers new data but not everything outstanding when loss was detected) as a sign that the next packet was also lost. The sender retransmits it at once and stays in fast recovery until a full acknowledgment arrives, tracked with a new variable called recover.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6582 obsoletes RFC 3782 and is the specification of NewReno for connections that cannot use SACK. The RFC also says the best alternative for multiple losses in a window is to use the SACK option when available.

facts.label: Minimum cwnd on full ACK (option 1 fix)

today: RFC 6582 is a Standards Track document that obsoletes RFC 3782, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the NewReno specification for TCP connections that cannot use SACK.

sections.title: The Problem with Reno Fast Recovery
sections.content:
In the Reno behavior described in RFC 5681, a TCP sender retransmits a packet only after a retransmit timeout, or after three duplicate acknowledgments trigger fast retransmit. A single timeout may resend several packets, but each fast retransmit resends just one.

That causes two problems when several packets are lost from a single window. First, Reno will often take a timeout. Second, even if it avoids the timeout, it can run multiple fast retransmits and window reductions.

If the SACK option is available, the sender knows which packets to resend. This document is for connections that cannot use SACK, either because the sender does not support it or because the peer did not indicate a willingness to use it.
sections.plainLanguage: If a few pieces of your message get lost, the old method only fixes one piece at a time and often gives up and waits a long time. This RFC is for the case where the helper that says exactly which pieces are missing is not available.

sections.title: Partial Acknowledgments and the recover Variable
sections.content:
Without SACK, the first new information after fast retransmit is the acknowledgment for the retransmitted packet. If only one packet was dropped, that acknowledgment covers everything sent before fast retransmit. If several were dropped, it covers some but not all of that data. The RFC calls this a partial acknowledgment.

The idea comes from Janey Hoe: on a partial acknowledgment, infer that the next in-sequence packet was lost and retransmit it. The RFC names the result NewReno, because it is a slight but significant variation of Reno.

The document adds one sender-side state variable, recover. While in fast recovery it records the send sequence number that must be acknowledged before fast recovery is declared over. The RFC assumes the reader knows SMSS, cwnd and FlightSize from RFC 5681.
sections.plainLanguage: If you get back some of your missing pages but not all of them, that tells you the next page is probably missing too. A sticky note called recover reminds you which page has to come back before you can stop asking.

sections.title: The NewReno Procedure
sections.content:
The procedures in Section 3.2 of RFC 5681 are followed, with four changes. The RFC deliberately avoids the RFC 2119 key words, because it gives sender-side guidance for performance and does not affect interoperability.

  • Initialization: recover is set to the initial send sequence number.
  • Third duplicate ACK: the sender checks whether the cumulative acknowledgment covers more than recover. If so, recover is set to the highest sequence number sent so far and the sender enters fast retransmit. If not, it does not enter fast retransmit and does not reset ssthresh.
  • New data acknowledged: a full acknowledgment covers everything up to and including recover. The sender deflates cwnd to either min(ssthresh, max(FlightSize, SMSS) + SMSS) or ssthresh and exits fast recovery. A partial acknowledgment makes the sender retransmit the first unacknowledged segment, deflate cwnd by the amount of new data acknowledged, add back SMSS bytes if at least one SMSS was acknowledged, send a new segment if cwnd permits, and stay in fast recovery. The first partial ACK also resets the retransmit timer.
  • Retransmit timeout: the highest sequence number sent is recorded in recover and the sender exits fast recovery if it was in it.

A cumulative acknowledgment of ack_number covers more than recover when ack_number - 1 > recover. If the second option is used for a full acknowledgment, the implementation is encouraged to avoid a burst of data, for example by limiting the packets sent in response to a single acknowledgment.
sections.plainLanguage: Each time a partly-good report comes back, the sender resends the next missing piece, sends a bit of new stuff if allowed, and keeps going. Only when everything up to the sticky-note spot is confirmed does it relax.

sections.title: Duplicate ACKs after a Timeout
sections.content:
After a retransmit timeout, the sender may get three duplicate acknowledgments that do not cover more than recover. This can mean it unnecessarily retransmitted at least three packets that the receiver already had, which is not new congestion. It can also mean a retransmitted packet was itself dropped. A NewReno sender that follows Section 3.2 does not infer a loss in this case, and the retransmit timer remains the backup.

The RFC describes two optional heuristics for telling the cases apart, and a sender may use one to enter fast retransmit in some cases anyway.

  • ACK heuristic: enter fast retransmit if cwnd is greater than SMSS bytes and the difference between highest_ack and prev_highest_ack is at most 4*SMSS bytes. It can fail if several ACKs are lost or the receiver does not send duplicate ACKs for out-of-order data.
  • Timestamp heuristic: enter fast retransmit if the echoed timestamp in the last non-duplicate acknowledgment equals the stored timestamp. It can fail if the receiver echoes timestamps arbitrarily or a timeout was spurious; detection algorithms such as Eifel (RFC 3522) can prevent the latter.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the sender hears the same complaint three times, but it is only because it sent extra copies by mistake. The RFC gives two optional tricks for guessing whether a piece is really missing or the sender is just hearing echoes.

sections.title: Notes for Receivers and Senders
sections.content:
For the receiver, RFC 5681 says out-of-order segments SHOULD be acknowledged immediately. Some receivers wait for the delayed acknowledgment timer before sending a partial acknowledgment, which severely limits the benefit of NewReno. The recommendation is to acknowledge immediately even when the out-of-order segment fills a hole.

For the sender, the RFC gives several pieces of advice.

  • Avoid a burst of data when leaving fast recovery, for example by limiting packets sent per acknowledgment (called maxburst_ in ns-2), by rate-based pacing, or by setting the slow start threshold to the resulting cwnd and resetting cwnd to FlightSize.
  • Use a separate flag to record whether the sender is in fast recovery, because the duplicate acknowledgment counter can be reset by window updates and out-of-order acknowledgments.
  • Update recover if sequence wraparound changes its ordering against the cumulative acknowledgment field.
  • Handle duplicate ACKs correctly when not in fast recovery, using Limited Transmit (RFC 3042) for the first two and the Section 4 guidance for three or more. Several NewReno implementations, including the one in ns-2, had a bug here that could cause a chain of spurious timeouts.
  • Do not update cwnd again after setting it on leaving fast recovery until a further event, such as an ACK arrival or timeout.
sections.plainLanguage: The one who receives should reply right away when a piece arrives, not wait around. The one who sends should not dump a huge pile of data all at once after recovering.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: RFC 5681 discusses the general security considerations for TCP congestion control. NewReno conforms with the congestion control requirements of RFC 5681, so those considerations apply here too. The RFC states there are no known additional security concerns for this algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: This change does not open any new doors for troublemakers beyond the ones TCP's congestion rules already have.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3782
sections.content:
RFC 6582 obsoletes RFC 3782, which in turn followed RFC 2582. Appendix B lists what changed.

In RFC 3782 the first full-ACK option for cwnd was min(ssthresh, FlightSize + SMSS). If FlightSize was zero, that gave 1 SMSS, so the sender could send only one segment, which may delay the receiver's acknowledgment because of delayed ACKs. FlightSize can be zero on a full ACK when the window is small, ACKs are lost, or a receive buffer runs short. The fix sets cwnd to at least 2*SMSS for option 1, so at least two segments are sent.

An editorial erratum on RFC 3782 is addressed in Section 6, and the specification text was rewritten to track Section 3.2 of RFC 5681. Sections 4, 5 and 9 to 11 of RFC 3782 were removed, with Appendix A pointing back to that material for retransmit timer variants, retransmission after partial ACKs, the motivation for recover, simulation test suites and a Reno versus NewReno comparison.
sections.plainLanguage: This edition fixes one small trap where the sender might send just one piece and then have to wait, and it tidies up the wording.

viz.caption: WHAT THE SENDER DOES ON NEW DATA ACKNOWLEDGED

cells: Everything up to and including recover
Set cwnd by one of two options and exit fast recovery
New data, but not all up to recover
Retransmit first unacknowledged segment, deflate cwnd, stay in fast recovery
